sections.title: From vague to scorable
paragraphs: Saying "this answer is better" is easy. Explaining *why* in a way another person — or an automated {{judge}} — can reproduce is harder. That is where a {{rubric}} comes in.

A {{rubric}} breaks quality into rows called {{criterion}}. Each row targets one measurable aspect: accuracy, tone, completeness, safety. Instead of a gut feeling, you score each row on a scale (often 1–5) with anchors that define what each level means.

The rubric is your shared language. Two reviewers can disagree on "helpfulness" until you write: "Score 5: answers the question fully with context. Score 3: answers but omits key details. Score 1: off-topic or incorrect."

In AiEval you will create evaluations with rubrics. Automation can score answers using these same {{criterion}} definitions — but only if the criteria are clear enough for a {{judge}} to apply consistently.
Next: how to draft rubric rows that travel well across {{model}}s and reviewers.
bullets: {{rubric}} — a scoring guide with multiple {{criterion}} rows.
{{criterion}} — one measurable aspect of quality (accuracy, tone, etc.).
Anchors: written definitions for each score level (1, 3, 5).

check.prompt: A team scores customer emails as "good" or "bad" but different reviewers disagree on half the emails. What is the fix?
check.answer: Write a rubric with clear criteria: what makes an email good vs bad?
choices: Train a bigger model and hope it guesses correctly
Write a rubric with clear criteria: what makes an email good vs bad?
Average all the scores and call it consensus
Only let one person score everything
check.explanation: Disagreement means the criteria are not defined. A {{rubric}} with explicit {{criterion}} rows and anchors aligns reviewers — and enables automation.

sections.title: Build rows, one criterion at a time
paragraphs: Start by listing what matters. For a support-answer task: accuracy, politeness, actionable next steps. For code generation: correctness, readability, security. Each aspect becomes a {{criterion}} row.

Then define anchors. Pick the top and bottom of your scale (5 and 1), and write concrete descriptions. "Score 5: code runs, passes tests, uses clear variable names. Score 1: syntax errors or fails tests." Middle scores (2, 3, 4) fill in between.
Click each task below to see example {{rubric}} rows. Notice how specific anchors make scoring predictable.
When drafting your own rubrics, test them: score a few real answers and see if the criteria are clear enough that you do not have to guess.

reveals.prompt: Task: Customer support reply. Criterion: Politeness. What are score anchors?
reveals.reveal: 5: Warm, empathetic, professional. 3: Neutral tone, no rudeness. 1: Dismissive, curt, or blames the customer.

reveals.prompt: Task: Essay grading. Criterion: Argument clarity. What are score anchors?
reveals.reveal: 5: Thesis is clear, evidence supports every claim. 3: Thesis stated but some claims lack support. 1: No clear thesis or unsupported assertions.

reveals.prompt: Task: Code review. Criterion: Security. What are score anchors?
reveals.reveal: 5: No known vulnerabilities, input validation present. 3: Minor issues, fixable quickly. 1: SQL injection risk or credentials in code.

check.prompt: You want to score {{model}} answers on "helpfulness." Which rubric row is clearest for reviewers to apply?
check.answer: 5: Answers question fully with context. 3: Answers but omits details. 1: Off-topic.
choices: Just write "helpful" or "not helpful" with no scale.
5: Answers question fully with context. 3: Answers but omits details. 1: Off-topic.
Ask the model to judge itself and trust the score.
check.explanation: Anchors with concrete definitions ("answers fully," "omits details," "off-topic") let reviewers score consistently. Vague labels like "good" or "okay" invite disagreement.

sections.title: Use your rubric to judge answers
paragraphs: Once the {{rubric}} is written, scoring is structured. Read the answer, check each {{criterion}} row, pick the anchor that fits best, record the score. Sum or average the rows to get an overall quality measure.

In AiEval's Compare page you will see answers scored row by row. If automation handled scoring, each {{criterion}} has a recorded score plus reasoning — you can spot-check whether the {{judge}} applied the rubric faithfully.

Good rubrics make disagreements debuggable. If two reviewers gave different scores, look at which {{criterion}} row caused the split and refine that anchor. If automation is off, adjust the {{judge}}'s prompt to reference the rubric more explicitly.
Next lesson: Structured outputs for judges — JSON scores automation can parse.
bullets: Score each {{criterion}} row separately, then combine.
Good rubrics let reviewers (and automation) score consistently.
Disagreements point to anchors that need sharpening.

aside.title: Try in AiEval
aside.body: On the create page, switch to custom {{criterion}} and draft rows with clear anchors before you run automation.

check.prompt: In one short phrase: what is a {{rubric}} in evaluation?
check.answer: A scoring guide with criteria and anchors
check.explanation: A {{rubric}} is a structured guide that breaks quality into {{criterion}} rows with explicit anchors for each score level.
